_about: Short descriptions written for the atlas for structures that have no text in Startup.blend and no Wikipedia article of their own. Standard textbook anatomy only (definitions, location, key contents). Merged by tools/postprocess_knowledge.py; never overrides the scene's own text. Please report errors.

fascia.Lateral intermuscular septum of arm: A sheet of deep fascia running from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus to the brachial fascia. It separates the anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm from the posterior (extensor) compartment and gives attachment to brachialis and brachioradialis in front and the triceps behind. The radial nerve and radial collateral artery pierce it on their way to the front of the elbow.
fascia.Lateral femoral intermuscular septum: A strong fascial partition between the lateral lip of the linea aspera of the femur and the fascia lata. It separates the anterior compartment of the thigh (vastus lateralis) from the posterior compartment (short head of biceps femoris).
fascia.Medial femoral intermuscular septum: A fascial partition running from the medial lip of the linea aspera of the femur to the fascia lata. It separates the anterior compartment of the thigh (vastus medialis) from the medial (adductor) compartment.

insertions.Quadriceps femoris muscle: Attachments of the quadriceps femoris. Its four heads (rectus femoris and the three vasti) unite in the quadriceps tendon, which attaches to the base of the patella; the pull continues through the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. Rectus femoris also arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine and the ilium above the acetabulum.
insertions.Rectus anterior capitis muscle: Attachments of rectus capitis anterior: it arises from the front of the lateral mass of the atlas (C1) and attaches to the basilar part of the occipital bone, in front of the foramen magnum.
insertions.Rectus lateralis capitis muscle: Attachments of rectus capitis lateralis: it arises from the upper surface of the transverse process of the atlas (C1) and attaches to the jugular process of the occipital bone.

regions.Antebrachial region: The forearm region, between the elbow and the wrist. It is divided into the anterior region of the forearm (over the flexor compartment) and the posterior region of the forearm (over the extensor compartment).
regions.Anterior region of ankle: The front of the ankle, over the talocrural joint. The tendons of tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus cross it beneath the extensor retinacula, together with the anterior tibial vessels and deep fibular nerve.
regions.Anterior region of arm: The front of the arm, between the shoulder and the elbow. It overlies the anterior (flexor) compartment: biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis, supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
regions.Anterior region of elbow: The front of the elbow. It contains the cubital fossa, through which pass the biceps tendon, the brachial artery and the median nerve; the median cubital vein crosses it superficially and is a common site for drawing blood.
regions.Anterior region of forearm: The front (palmar) surface of the forearm, overlying the anterior compartment: the pronators and the flexors of the wrist and fingers.
regions.Anterior region of knee: The front of the knee, centred on the patella and the patellar ligament. The prepatellar bursae lie in front of the patella.
regions.Anterior region of leg: The front of the leg, between the knee and the ankle. The anterior border and medial surface of the tibia (the shin) are directly under the skin; lateral to them lies the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior and the long toe extensors).
regions.Anterior region of thigh: The front of the thigh. It overlies the anterior compartment (quadriceps femoris and sartorius) and, at its upper end, the femoral triangle with the femoral nerve, artery and vein.
regions.Anterior region of wrist: The palmar side of the wrist. The tendons of the wrist and finger flexors pass here; the radial pulse is felt on its lateral side, lateral to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis.
regions.Apex of auricle: The highest point of the helix of the external ear.
regions.Brachial region: The arm proper, between the shoulder and the elbow. It is divided into anterior and posterior regions of the arm.
regions.Carpal region: The wrist region, between the forearm and the hand. It is divided into the anterior (palmar) and posterior (dorsal) regions of the wrist.
regions.Cubital region: The elbow region. Its anterior part contains the cubital fossa; its posterior part is centred on the olecranon, with the ulnar nerve palpable behind the medial epicondyle.
regions.Distal transverse arch of foot: The transverse curvature of the foot at the level of the heads of the metatarsals. It is shallow and flattens under load, as all five metatarsal heads take weight.
regions.Proximal transverse arch of foot: The transverse arch of the foot at the level of the cuneiforms, the cuboid and the bases of the metatarsals. It is maintained by the wedge shape of these bones, the interosseous and plantar ligaments, and the tendons of fibularis longus and tibialis posterior.
regions.Dorsal surfaces of digits of foot: The upper surfaces of the toes. The toenails lie on the dorsal surfaces of the distal phalanges.
regions.Dorsal surfaces of digits of hand: The back surfaces of the fingers. The fingernails lie on the dorsal surfaces of the distal phalanges.
regions.Dorsum of foot: The upper surface of the foot. The dorsal venous arch lies here, and the pulse of the dorsalis pedis artery can be felt lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus.
regions.Dorsum of hand: The back of the hand. The dorsal venous network, a common site for cannulation, and the extensor tendons of the fingers are visible under the thin skin.
regions.Eminentia conchae: The bulge on the cranial (back) surface of the auricle that corresponds to the concha on its lateral surface.
regions.Eminentia fossae triangularis: The elevation on the cranial (back) surface of the auricle that corresponds to the triangular fossa on its lateral surface.
regions.Eminentia scaphae: The elevation on the cranial (back) surface of the auricle that corresponds to the scapha on its lateral surface.
regions.Femoral region: The thigh, between the hip and the knee. It is divided into the anterior and posterior regions of the thigh; the femoral triangle lies in the upper anterior part.
regions.Gluteal region: The buttock, between the iliac crest above and the gluteal fold below. It overlies the gluteal muscles; the sciatic nerve passes through its lower medial part, which is why intramuscular injections are given in the upper lateral quadrant.
regions.Greater supraclavicular fossa: The depression above the middle of the clavicle, lateral to the sternocleidomastoid. It overlies the omoclavicular (subclavian) triangle: the pulse of the subclavian artery and the trunks of the brachial plexus can be felt here.
regions.Hairs of eyebrow: The short, thick hairs of the eyebrows (supercilia), which grow from the skin over the superciliary arches.
regions.Hallucial eminence: The rounded prominence on the medial part of the sole at the base of the great toe, formed by the short muscles of the great toe (abductor hallucis and flexor hallucis brevis) over the head of the first metatarsal.
regions.Heel region: The back of the foot, over the calcaneus. The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon attaches to the back of the calcaneus just above it.
regions.Hip region: The region around the hip joint (coxal region). Laterally the greater trochanter of the femur can be felt under the skin.
regions.Infra-orbital region: The part of the face below the orbit, beside the nose and above the upper lip. The infra-orbital nerve and vessels emerge here from the infra-orbital foramen.
regions.Interscapular region: The part of the upper back between the two scapulae.
regions.Knee region: The region of the knee. Its anterior part is centred on the patella; its posterior part is the popliteal fossa.
regions.Lateral bicipital groove: The furrow along the lateral side of biceps brachii in the arm. The cephalic vein runs in it.
regions.Lateral border of foot: The little-toe side of the foot. The tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal can be felt about halfway along it.
regions.Lateral border of forearm: The radial (thumb-side) border of the forearm.
regions.Medial border of foot: The great-toe side of the foot, along which the medial longitudinal arch rises.
regions.Medial border of forearm: The ulnar (little-finger-side) border of the forearm.
regions.Lateral part of longitudinal arch of foo: The low, flat lateral part of the longitudinal arch, formed by the calcaneus, the cuboid and the fourth and fifth metatarsals. It rests almost on the ground when standing.
regions.Medial part of longitudinal arch of foot: The higher medial part of the longitudinal arch, formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, the three cuneiforms and the first three metatarsals. The head of the talus is its keystone; it is supported by the plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament, the plantar aponeurosis and the tendon of tibialis posterior.
regions.Lateral retromalleolar region: The region behind the lateral malleolus. The tendons of fibularis longus and brevis pass here, with the sural nerve and the small saphenous vein.
regions.Medial retromalleolar region: The region behind the medial malleolus. The tendons of tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus pass here with the posterior tibial artery and the tibial nerve (tarsal tunnel); the posterior tibial pulse is felt here.
regions.Metatarsal region: The middle part of the foot, over the five metatarsal bones.
regions.Nail plate: The hard, translucent plate of keratin on the dorsal surface of the distal phalanx of a finger.
regions.Nail plate (foot): The hard plate of keratin (toenail) on the dorsal surface of the distal phalanx of a toe.
regions.Palmar surfaces of digits of hand: The palm-side surfaces of the fingers, with the creases over the interphalangeal joints and the finger pads.
regions.Parotideomasseteric region: The side of the face in front of the ear and over the ramus of the mandible, overlying the parotid gland and the masseter muscle.
regions.Posterior region of ankle: The back of the ankle, centred on the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
regions.Posterior region of arm: The back of the arm, overlying the posterior compartment (triceps brachii). The radial nerve winds around the humerus here in the radial groove.
regions.Posterior region of elbow: The back of the elbow, centred on the olecranon of the ulna. The ulnar nerve lies in the groove behind the medial epicondyle.
regions.Posterior region of forearm: The back (dorsal) surface of the forearm, overlying the posterior compartment: the extensors of the wrist and fingers and the supinator.
regions.Posterior region of knee: The back of the knee, containing the popliteal fossa with the popliteal artery and vein and the tibial and common fibular nerves.
regions.Posterior region of leg: The back of the leg (calf or sural region), overlying the posterior compartment, chiefly the triceps surae (gastrocnemius and soleus).
regions.Posterior region of thigh: The back of the thigh, overlying the hamstring muscles and the sciatic nerve.
regions.Posterior region of wrist: The back of the wrist. The extensor tendons pass beneath the extensor retinaculum; the anatomical snuffbox lies on its lateral side.
regions.Radial foveola: The anatomical snuffbox: the hollow on the lateral side of the wrist between the tendons of extensor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, seen when the thumb is extended. The scaphoid is felt in its floor and the radial artery crosses it.
regions.Regions of digits of foot: The surface regions of the toes: their dorsal and plantar surfaces.
regions.Regions of digits of hand: The surface regions of the fingers: their dorsal and palmar surfaces.
regions.Regions of foot: The surface regions of the foot: the heel, the dorsum, the sole, its borders and the toes.
regions.Regions of hand: The surface regions of the hand: the palm, the dorsum and the fingers.
regions.Regions of lower limb: The surface regions of the lower limb: gluteal, hip, thigh, knee, leg, ankle and foot regions.
regions.Sole: The plantar surface of the foot. Its thick skin is bound down to the underlying plantar aponeurosis, which helps support the longitudinal arch.
regions.Talocrural region: The ankle region, around the talocrural joint. It includes the anterior and posterior regions of the ankle and the retromalleolar regions.
regions.Leg region: The leg (crural region), between the knee and the ankle. It is divided into anterior and posterior regions of the leg.
regions.Perionyx: A thin band of epidermis, a remnant of the embryonic eponychium, that may persist across the proximal part of the nail plate.
regions.Perionyx (foot): A thin band of epidermis, a remnant of the embryonic eponychium, that may persist across the proximal part of the toenail.

skeletal.Anterior cells of ethmoid bone: The anterior group of ethmoidal air cells, small air spaces within the labyrinth of the ethmoid bone between the nasal cavity and the orbit. They drain into the middle nasal meatus.
skeletal.Middle cells of ethmoid bone: The middle group of ethmoidal air cells in the labyrinth of the ethmoid bone. They drain into the middle nasal meatus, on or above the ethmoidal bulla.
skeletal.Posterior cells of ethmoid bone: The posterior group of ethmoidal air cells in the labyrinth of the ethmoid bone. They drain into the superior nasal meatus.
skeletal.Bones of free part of lower limb: The bones of the lower limb below the hip bone: femur, patella, tibia, fibula, the seven tarsal bones, five metatarsals and fourteen phalanges.
skeletal.Skeleton of upper limbs: The bones of the upper limb: the pectoral girdle (clavicle and scapula) and the free limb (humerus, radius, ulna, eight carpal bones, five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges).
skeletal.Teeth: The adult (permanent) dentition has 32 teeth: in each half of each jaw two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. Children have 20 deciduous (milk) teeth.
skeletal.Costal cartilage of first rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that continues the first rib forward to the manubrium of the sternum. Its joint with the manubrium is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis), so it allows almost no movement.
skeletal.Costal cartilage of second rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the second rib to the sternum at the sternal angle, where it articulates with both the manubrium and the body of the sternum. The sternal angle is the landmark for counting ribs.
skeletal.Costal cartilage of third rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the third rib to the body of the sternum (a true rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of fourth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the fourth rib to the body of the sternum (a true rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of fifth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the fifth rib to the body of the sternum (a true rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of sixth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the sixth rib to the body of the sternum (a true rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of seventh rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage that joins the seventh rib to the lower body of the sternum, near the xiphisternal junction. It is the last cartilage to reach the sternum (the seventh is the last true rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of eighth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage of the eighth rib. It does not reach the sternum but joins the cartilage above it, forming part of the costal margin (a false rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of ninth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage of the ninth rib. It joins the cartilage above it and forms part of the costal margin (a false rib).
skeletal.Costal cartilage of tenth rib: The bar of hyaline cartilage of the tenth rib. It joins the cartilage above it and forms the lowest part of the costal margin (a false rib).

visceral.(Accessory parotid gland): A small detached part of the parotid gland, present in many people, lying on the masseter above the parotid duct, into which it drains.
visceral.Extrahepatic bile ducts: The bile passages outside the liver. The right and left hepatic ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct, which is joined by the cystic duct from the gallbladder to form the bile duct. The bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct and opens into the second part of the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla.
visceral.Hypophysis: The pituitary gland. It sits in the hypophysial fossa of the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone and hangs from the hypothalamus by the infundibulum. Its anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) release hormones that control many other endocrine glands.
visceral.Left medial segment of liver (IV): Segment IV of the liver in the Couinaud classification. It belongs to the functional left liver and lies between the plane of the middle hepatic vein and the umbilical fissure (falciform ligament). Its lower part includes the quadrate lobe.
visceral.Mucosa of nasal cavity: The lining of the nasal cavity. Most of it is respiratory mucosa (ciliated epithelium with mucous glands and a rich venous plexus) that warms, moistens and filters the inspired air; the roof carries the olfactory mucosa.
visceral.Superior parathyroid gland: The upper of the two pairs of parathyroid glands, small endocrine glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, usually near the level of the cricoid cartilage. They secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium.
visceral.Tracheobronchial tree: The branching system of conducting airways: the trachea divides into the right and left main bronchi, which branch into lobar and segmental bronchi and then into ever smaller bronchioles.
